title: Throwing a stoneware batter bowl with spout
subtitle: A wide, lipped mixing bowl with a pulled pouring spout and helper handle, thrown in smooth stoneware at cone 6
excerpt: A batter bowl is a wide, deep mixing bowl with a pouring spout and a gripping handle for one-handed control at the stovetop. It is thrown as an open cylinder, then shaped out into a broad bowl, with the spout pulled from the rim lip and a solid pulled handle attached at the leather-hard stage. The result is one of the most functional pieces a potter can make for a working kitchen.
sourceNotes: Batter bowl throwing pattern derived from first principles. Pulled-spout rim technique documented in Bernard Leach, A Potter's Book (1940, Faber). V&A open-access collection for batter bowl form references.

glossaryTerms.definition: The working stage where clay holds its shape but remains damp enough to trim, join, and attach handles
Air-dried but unfired; fragile, ready for bisque firing
The first firing, around cone 06 (1000 degrees Celsius), that hardens greenware into porous bisqueware ready for glaze

content.text: A batter bowl is a deep, wide mixing vessel with a prominent lip at one point of the rim for pouring, and a sturdy gripping handle set opposite. It earns its place in a kitchen through daily use: mixing pancake batter, pouring into muffin tins, transferring stock. The throwing starts as an open, slightly outward-flared cylinder, then widens into the bowl shape before the rim is lipped and the handle is attached at the
leather-hard
stage.

The finished bowl is approximately 20 cm in diameter and 10 cm deep, throwing from 900 g of smooth stoneware. At intermediate level, the skill point is controlling a wide, open form without letting the walls collapse outward, then pulling a clean lipped spout from the rim without distorting the rest of the rim line.

attrs.title: Studio safety
attrs.content: Silica dust is the chronic studio hazard. Silicosis is irreversible. Mix wet whenever possible. Wear a P100 respirator any time raw glaze powders are open. Wet-clean only: no sweeping, no compressed air, no dry sanding indoors. Ventilation matters: a downdraft vent or open window with an extractor. Wear welder's shade-5 glasses when peephole-watching at high temperatures. Never open a hot kiln below 80 degrees Celsius. Keep a Class A fire extinguisher within reach.

content.text: What you'll need

materials.name: Small piece of stoneware for handle
Mid-fire glaze, pre-mixed
materials.quantity: enough to glaze interior and exterior

content.text: Preparation

Wedge 900 g of smooth stoneware thoroughly until the clay has an even, bubble-free texture. A well-wedged lump centres more readily and throws without air pockets. Fix a bat onto the wheel head: a batter bowl is wide enough that cutting it off the bare wheel head risks distorting the rim. The bat gives you a solid base to lift the piece clear on. Set aside a small extra lump of 150 g wrapped in plastic for the handle: you will pull the handle as a separate piece and attach it at the leather-hard stage.
Throwing the bowl

Centre the 900 g of stoneware on the bat at medium speed. Use firm, even palm pressure from above and the heel of one hand from the side. The clay should spin without any visible wobble before you open it.

Open the floor wide: press two fingers down the centre and pull outward to a floor diameter of 130 mm. Leave 8 to 10 mm of clay at the base. Keeping the floor wide from the start is the key to a roomy bowl interior.
Pull the walls upward in two passes, keeping the walls at 6 to 7 mm thick. Aim for a straight-sided cylinder about 12 cm tall at this stage, with a rim diameter of 130 mm to match the floor.

On the third pass, begin to flare the walls outward: place the outside hand slightly lower than the inside hand and push the wall gently outward as you pull upward. The rim should open to 180 to 200 mm. Do not rush the flare or the wall will buckle.

Refine the bowl profile with a wooden rib held against the outside, compressing and smoothing the wall. Keep the base generous so the bowl sits solidly. The finished wall thickness at the rim should be 5 mm; thicker at the base to allow trimming.

To create the pouring spout: with the wheel stationary, use a wetted thumb and index finger to pinch the rim at one point into a short lipped projection. Pull the clay gently outward and down to form a small V-shaped channel about 30 mm wide. The lip should be level with the original rim height, not lifted up.
Smooth the rim with the chamois leather, working around the circumference and finishing at the edges of the spout without dragging the spout shape.
Cut the bowl off the bat with a wire cutter. Leave it on the bat. Cover loosely with plastic and dry to leather-hard before trimming.
Pulling and attaching the handle

While the bowl dries toward leather-hard, pull the handle from the reserved 150 g lump. Take the lump in one hand. Wet the other hand and pull firmly downward from the base of the lump with a light grip, rotating slightly with each pull. Repeat until you have a strap about 14 cm long, 25 mm wide at the top, tapering to 15 mm at the tip, and 8 mm thick throughout. Hang the pulled strap over the edge of the wheel head or a dowel rod to set a gentle curve into it while the bowl finishes drying. Attach the handle when both bowl and handle are at leather-hard: score both attachment surfaces, apply a dab of water, press firmly, and smooth the junction with a finger.
Trimming
At
leather-hard
, centre the bowl upside-down on the wheel head. Use pottery clay coils pressed around the rim to hold it steady.

Use calipers to mark a foot ring at 110 mm diameter on the base. Trim a foot ring 6 mm tall and 6 mm wide using the loop tool. Clear clay from inside the foot ring to a depth that matches the wall thickness, leaving an even 6 to 7 mm base.
Smooth the foot ring edges with a damp sponge. Check the outside curve of the bowl from base to rim: trim away any excess clay at the lower third of the outside to give a graceful continuous curve.
Drying
Once the handle is attached and the foot ring trimmed, dry the bowl slowly to
bone-dry

. Wide open forms and handles dry at different rates: cover the bowl loosely with light plastic for the first 24 hours to even out drying, then uncover and let the piece air-dry completely. Drying on a wire rack allows air underneath the foot ring, which helps prevent the base drying faster than the walls and cracking.
Bisque firing
Load the bone-dry bowl upright on a kiln shelf with adequate space around it.
Bisque

fire to cone 06 (1000 degrees Celsius). Use a slow ramp: 60 degrees Celsius per hour to 120 degrees Celsius to drive off all residual moisture, then 100 degrees Celsius per hour to cone 06. Hold for 10 minutes at peak. Allow the kiln to cool fully before opening.
Glazing and glaze firing

Glaze the interior first: pour glaze in, swirl to coat all inner surfaces fully, then pour out. For a kitchen mixing bowl, a pale satin or glossy food-safe glaze on the interior gives the most practical finish. Glaze the exterior by dipping or brushing, leaving the foot ring and base free of glaze. Clean any glaze from the foot ring and a 5 mm band around the base with a damp sponge before loading. Glaze-fire to cone 6 (1220 degrees Celsius). A slow final ramp of 60 degrees Celsius per hour above 1100 degrees Celsius reduces the risk of thermal shock in the wide form.
Care

Cone 6 stoneware fired to maturity is dense, non-porous, and food-safe with a lead-free glaze. The batter bowl is dishwasher-safe and suitable for daily use. It is not designed for stovetop or direct-flame use: stoneware transfers heat slowly and thermal shock from a direct flame can crack the base. Use it for mixing and pouring at room temperature and refrigerator-to-table transfer only.
Variations

A smaller batter bowl from 500 g of clay at 14 cm diameter is well-suited to whisking salad dressings or sauces in small quantities. The proportions of the spout and handle should scale with the bowl: a smaller handle at 10 cm length keeps the visual balance.

Adding a pressed-in measuring scale on the inside wall is a practical touch. At the leather-hard stage, use a needle tool to incise horizontal lines at 250 ml, 500 ml, and 1 litre marks before bisque firing. The lines survive the glaze firing and remain readable as incised marks beneath the glaze surface.

For a decorative finish, apply a contrasting coloured slip to the exterior before trimming. Let it reach leather-hard. Then wax the exterior. Dip the interior in a clear liner glaze. The slip colour shows through the clear coat on the outside. The interior stays fully sealed and food-safe.

rows.cause: Flare attempted too early before the walls had enough upward height to support the shape change
rows.fix: Get the full height in the cylinder stage first, then flare on the final pass only. Slow the wheel speed when opening the form wide.

rows.problem: Spout pulls the rim out of round
rows.cause: Wheel was still spinning when the spout was pulled
rows.fix: Stop the wheel completely before pinching the spout. Work slowly with wetted fingers on a stationary rim.

rows.problem: Handle cracks at the join after drying
rows.cause: Handle and bowl were at different moisture levels when joined, or the join was not fully compressed
rows.fix: Join handle to bowl when both are at the same leather-hard stage. Score both surfaces generously, add water, press firmly, and smooth the junction from both sides.

rows.problem: Foot ring trims unevenly around the circumference
rows.cause: Bowl not centred accurately when inverted for trimming
rows.fix: Use the tap-centring method: spin the wheel slowly and tap the upturned base toward the centre until no wobble is visible before engaging the loop tool.

rows.problem: Glaze pools in the spout channel and runs during firing
rows.cause: Too much glaze applied to the spout area
rows.fix: Thin the glaze coat around the spout lip with a damp brush before firing, or leave the outer face of the spout unglazed and glaze only the interior-facing channel surface.
